seo.title: Luigi Footprints Foundation | Community-led conservation in Kenya
seo.description: A Kenyan foundation protecting wildlife by empowering the communities who live alongside it: education, tree nurseries, women's enterprise and human-wildlife coexistence in the Amboseli ecosystem, Nairobi National Park and the Samburu National Reserve.

blocks.title: Protecting wildlife by empowering communities
blocks.subtitle: Community-led conservation in Kenya, from the Amboseli ecosystem to Nairobi National Park and the Samburu National Reserve.
blocks.content: In the heart of Kenya, where elephants still follow ancient migration routes and communities have lived alongside wildlife for generations, the future of people and nature is deeply connected. We believe conservation is not simply about protecting animals. It is about creating opportunity, restoring dignity, and giving communities the means to build sustainable futures. When communities thrive, wildlife thrives too.

image.alt: A herd of elephants walking among acacia trees, cattle egrets at their feet

blocks.title: What we believe
blocks.subtitle: Dignity for communities is equal to protection for wildlife.
blocks.content:
For too long, conservation has been treated as something separate from people's everyday lives. Our experience shows the opposite. The communities living closest to wildlife are not obstacles to conservation. They are its greatest partners.

When young people receive an education, they become the next conservation leaders. When women earn an income, families become more resilient. When landscapes are restored, wildlife and people both benefit. And when people feel included and respected, conservation lasts.

image.alt: Young volunteers planting mangrove seedlings at the Kenyan coast

seo.title: About | Luigi Francescon's legacy and our trustees
seo.description: The Luigi Footprints Foundation was founded in memory of Luigi Francescon. Read his story, what guides the foundation, and meet the Board of Trustees.

blocks.title: Our story
blocks.subtitle: Founded in memory of Luigi Francescon, whose love for Kenya, its wildlife and its people still guides the work.
blocks.content: Growing up near Nairobi National Park, Luigi knew a Kenya where wildlife moved freely across the landscape and nature was an everyday part of life. Those early years gave him a lifelong respect for the natural world and a deep concern for the wellbeing of the generations to come.

image.alt: Foundation members and supporters gathered beside a Walk for Elephants vehicle

blocks.title: The legacy
blocks.subtitle: He understood that conservation and human development are inseparable.
blocks.content:
Wildlife cannot survive if communities are struggling. Communities cannot thrive if the ecosystems they depend on are lost.

After Luigi's passing in 2016, the foundation was created to carry that understanding forward: protecting wildlife while creating opportunities for children, families and communities across Kenya. Today it works through practical, community-led programmes in the Amboseli ecosystem, Nairobi National Park and the Samburu National Reserve.

image.alt: Visitors and community members planting trees in Nairobi National Park

blocks.content: Protecting wildlife and uplifting communities were never opposing forces. They are two sides of the same footprint.
blocks.subtitle: Luigi Francescon, 1948–2016

items.title: Mission
items.description: To create thriving communities that take an active part in conserving wildlife and natural ecosystems, through education, economic empowerment, sustainable livelihoods and environmental stewardship.

items.title: Vision
items.description: A world where empowered communities and healthy ecosystems coexist, securing a sustainable future for the generations to come.

items.title: Philosophy
items.description: Dignity for communities is equal to protection for wildlife. When young people are educated, women earn an income and landscapes are restored, conservation becomes a natural, community-led choice.

blocks.title: Board of Trustees
blocks.subtitle: The people responsible for the foundation's governance and for its work on the ground.

items.name: Annabella Francescon
items.bio: For Annabella, wildlife conservation and youth engagement are lifelong callings. Growing up, she witnessed a raw, untouched Kenya when traveling between Nairobi and Mombasa meant going on a true dirt-track safari surrounded by thousands of migrating elephants. Mesmerized by these special creatures, elephants became her emblem animal, sparking decades of dedicated support for the survival of elephants, rhinos, and African wildlife. Alongside her environmental focus, Annabella finds immense joy in working with young people, firmly believing that the future belongs to their exuberance. She is passionately committed to providing youth with the formal and practical education they need to confidently navigate the world ahead.

image.alt: Annabella Francescon, Chairman

items.name: Peter Mwangi Karanja
items.bio: Born and raised in Loitokitok on the picturesque slopes of Mt. Kilimanjaro, Peter has spent his entire life alongside the spectacular wildlife of Amboseli National Park and Tsavo West. His journey began as an active member of the Wildlife Clubs of Kenya, which paved the way for a fulfilling career in the tourism industry. Over the years, working with renowned conservationists like Annabella, Pat Awori, Cynthia Moss, and Jonathan Scott deepened his appreciation for our planet's irreplaceable habitats. Having stood on the frontlines against the poaching crises of the 1990s and 2000s, Peter believes collective action can overcome any threat. Today, alarmed by the destruction of local forests, he channels his urgency into aggressive tree-planting initiatives, helping the foundation restore ecosystems little by little—or as the Swahili say, 'Kidogo Kidogo Hujaza Kibaba.'

image.alt: Peter Mwangi Karanja, Secretary

items.name: Jose Manuel Lapena Casamayor
items.bio: Years ago, Jose Manuel traveled to Kenya for the first time with Annabella as his guide. That transformative trip introduced him to a pristine, natural world thriving in close proximity to the wildlife he had always dreamed of experiencing. From that exact moment, he realized the urgent global responsibility to preserve these wild landscapes for future generations. Having returned to Africa numerous times since, that initial feeling has only grown stronger, driving his unwavering commitment to leverage his financial oversight skills to support and conserve our natural planet.

image.alt: Jose Manuel Lapena Casamayor, Treasurer

items.name: Daniel Muturi Gatumbo
items.bio: Daniel's path to conservation came through a gradual, powerful awareness of how human actions can inadvertently harm our planet. As a primary school student, he loved the hands-on responsibility of planting trees and grass to heal bare, eroded hillsides. Haunted by childhood stories of extinct creatures like dinosaurs, he often wondered what would happen if mankind turned the world into a barren desert. This early curiosity evolved into a professional mission when he entered the tourism industry, realizing that his livelihood, and the livelihood of his community, is entirely dependent on keeping Kenya's natural scenery and wildlife safe, vibrant, and accessible.

image.alt: Daniel Muturi Gatumbo, Operations Coordinator

items.name: Justin Chuma Kenya
items.bio: Raised on the lush, green slopes of Mount Kenya, Chuma watched with a heavy heart as domestic and commercial deforestation stripped away over fifty percent of his childhood landscape. Refusing to remain a bystander, he joined environmental clubs throughout his school and college years to restore the natural beauty he remembered. His deep passion for indigenous trees led him to mobilize local communities and authorities to plant more trees than were being lost. Today, Chuma uses his accounting expertise to ensure the foundation's resources are perfectly balanced to combat the real-world threats of global warming and environmental degradation.

image.alt: Justin Chuma Kenya, Accountant

seo.title: Our work | Education, restoration, enterprise and coexistence
seo.description: Four programmes in Kenya: scholarships and the Amboseli OYC Choir, the Olchani tree nurseries, Dignity Tailors and Maasai beadwork enterprise, and coexistence tools including Dignity Housing for rangers.

blocks.title: Our work
blocks.subtitle: Practical, community-led programmes in the Amboseli ecosystem, Nairobi National Park and the Samburu National Reserve.
blocks.content: We work face to face with the people who live alongside wildlife, designing programmes that answer the real, everyday challenges of doing so, and making sure conservation brings tangible social and economic value.

image.alt: Volunteers with collection bags during a clean-up at Lake Nakuru National Park

blocks.title: Education and youth
blocks.subtitle: Educating the next generation of conservation leaders.
blocks.content:
The future of conservation depends on the young people who will inherit it. Across the Amboseli ecosystem we fund secondary school scholarships and run conservation workshops, mentorship and environmental awareness programmes that help young people understand their role in protecting the world around them. Our programmes have reached thousands of students so far.

The Amboseli OYC Choir is one of the most inspiring. Young people use music, dance and poetry to carry messages of conservation, culture and coexistence into their own communities.

image.alt: Students sitting an exam in a Kenyan classroom

blocks.title: Landscape restoration
blocks.subtitle: The Olchani Project: restoring landscapes, one tree at a time.
blocks.content:
Healthy ecosystems support healthy communities. Through the Olchani Project we restore degraded land, strengthen wildlife corridors and help communities become stewards of their own environment.

Tree planting is not simply putting seedlings in the ground. It rebuilds ecosystems, improves climate resilience and creates livelihoods. Working with local communities, we have established four community-managed nurseries with capacity for 42,000 indigenous seedlings, creating work and skills for women and young people.

image.alt: Indigenous seedlings being unloaded for a community planting day

blocks.title: Community enterprise
blocks.subtitle: Creating opportunities for the people who live with wildlife.
blocks.content:
Conservation succeeds when families can see its benefits in daily life. The Dignity Tailors programme gives women skills training, craftsmanship and a route into business. The Inkaramatak Ildepen Maasai Ushanga shop lets Maasai women sell their beadwork directly to travellers and keep the value of their work. Tourism partnerships invite visitors to take part in conservation activities while supporting local livelihoods.

Stronger household incomes make communities active partners in protecting wildlife and the land it depends on.

image.alt: A farmer harvesting cabbages during the COVID-19 livelihoods project

blocks.title: Coexistence and guarding
blocks.subtitle: Helping people and wildlife share the same land, and supporting the rangers who protect it.
blocks.content:
For communities near protected areas, encounters with predators and elephants can threaten livestock, crops and lives. Rather than choose between people and wildlife, we work on solutions that serve both: predator-deterrent lighting that protects homesteads, and beekeeping that earns an income while discouraging elephants from entering settlements.

Behind every protected landscape are rangers who spend long periods away from home in remote conditions. Through the Dignity Housing project we are replacing tents with safe, self-contained homes for the rhino rangers of Nairobi National Park. Four of the park's 25 ranger camps have been housed so far.

image.alt: Trustee Annabella Francescon inside a completed Dignity House for rangers

blocks.subtitle: In short
blocks.content: Four programmes, one approach. Scholarships and the Amboseli OYC Choir keep young people in school and give them a voice. The Olchani Project puts restoration in local hands, with four community-run nurseries for 42,000 indigenous seedlings. Dignity Tailors and the Maasai Ushanga shop turn craft into income that stays at home, and lighting, beekeeping and Dignity Housing make it safer to live alongside wildlife. None of it is done for communities. All of it is done with them.

blocks.title: Our impact
blocks.subtitle: When communities thrive, wildlife thrives.
blocks.content: Every project we take on is built around a simple idea: lasting conservation happens when communities are empowered to lead it. The impact reaches beyond numbers. It is a student staying in school, a family earning a steady income, a ranger returning to a safe home, and a landscape beginning to recover.

blocks.title: When nature needs us most
blocks.subtitle: Emergency response during drought and invasion.
blocks.content:
Conservation needs long-term commitment, but it also demands action in a crisis. During severe droughts we have worked with wildlife authorities to truck emergency water and deliver hay to wildlife struggling to survive.

We have supported the removal of the invasive Parthenium weed that chokes grazing land, and worked alongside communities to restore degraded habitat.

projects.title: Dignity Housing for wildlife rangers
projects.excerpt: The Luigi Footprints Foundation has developed a project called Dignity Housing whereby we are preparing self-contained container homes for these very deserving rangers who put their lives out in the wild to save and care for our wildlife. Each home will have 3 beds, a small kitchenette, a shower and flush toilet, solar power for lighting and for hot water, and large water tanks to cater to all their needs.
projects.content:
Inside the Nairobi National Park, there are 25 camps where rangers live in order to secure all the areas of the park to control the wellbeing, in particular, of the 125 rhinos and, indeed, all the wildlife within. These rangers have been living in basic tents.

The Luigi Footprints Foundation has developed a project called Dignity Housing whereby we are preparing self-contained container homes for these very deserving rangers who put their lives out in the wild to save and care for our wildlife. Each home will have 3 beds, a small kitchenette, a shower and flush toilet, solar power for lighting and for hot water, and large water tanks to cater to all their needs.

We have, so far, built 4 of these homes, with another 21 more camps inside the Nairobi National Park to bring the Dignity Houses to, in order to have all these special rangers well housed. Each one of these fully fitted homes costs US$ 14,000.00.

We need your help to have all 25 units of our Dignity Housing in place. Any small donation will be much appreciated. If a whole unit is funded we will have a plaque put onto the home with your name or the name of your organization on it.
